newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House panel to interview 150 on funds scandal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House panel to interview 150 on funds scandal.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

The chairman of a House of Representatives committee investigating campaign fund raising scandals in the 1996 U.S. presidential election moved on Tuesday to take wide powers to interview witnesses and issue subpoenas.

Dan Burton, Republican chairman of the Government Reform and Oversight Committee, called a meeting to grant him the ability to allow committee staff to take legal depositions of witnesses and apply for the assistance of foreign courts to conduct interviews with witnesses overseas.

The committee was expected to approve the request along party lines over the angry opposition of Democrats, who said they would argue that Burton was voting himself unprecedented powers. The meeting, originally scheduled for Tuesday, was postponed until Wednesday to allow all members to attend.
If, as expected, the committee approved Burton's request, it would need to be confirmed by the Rules Committee and by the full House of Representatives, possibly later this week.

The committee was probing whether Asian business interests or the Chinese government tried to influence the 1996 presidential election by illegally donating funds to the Democratic Party through Asian-American intermediaries.
It was also investigating whether foreigners won influence, were granted favours or gained access to classified information in return for their alleged illegal financial support.
A Senate committee as well as a Justice Department task force were also investigating the 1996 elections.
Many key witnesses have either taken refuge in Asian countries or invoked their right under the Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution to refuse to answer questions.

One key witness, former Commerce Department official and Democratic Party fund raiser John Huang, told a Chinese American audience in New York on Sunday that he would cooperate with the investigation.

But committee staff members said that when they spoke to Huang's lawyer to check his statement, they were told Huang had either been misquoted or misinterpreted and he still intended to "take the fifth".
Burton said investigators needed to interview between 150 and 200 witnesses. The size of the task made it necessary for him to request the new powers.
